cls: Tetracycline-class antibacterial (also used off-label for SIADH)
pharm: Bacteriostatic tetracycline that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; its renal action of inducing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is exploited off-label to correct hyponatraemia in SIADH

Take on empty stomach 1 h before or 2 h after food; avoid dairy/antacids/iron
Contraindicated - tetracyclines cause fetal harm and tooth/bone effects
Avoid - excreted in milk; risk of tooth staining and effects on infant
Use cautiously; reduce dose/extend interval - accumulation, azotaemia, anti-anabolic effect
Use cautiously and reduce dose; tetracyclines can be hepatotoxic
No specific interaction; avoid excess in hepatic impairment
Renal and hepatic function on prolonged use; serum sodium when used for SIADH
summary: Demeclocycline is a long-acting tetracycline-class antibacterial that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and is indicated for infections caused by susceptible organisms including rickettsiae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Borrelia, and as an alternative where penicillin is contraindicated. The usual adult dose is 150 mg four times daily or 300 mg twice daily (about 600 mg/day). Like other tetracyclines it should not be used during tooth development (latter half of pregnancy, infancy and children under 8 years) because it causes permanent tooth discoloration and can affect bone growth, and it causes a pronounced phototoxic (exaggerated sunburn) reaction. Demeclocycline characteristically induces reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, an effect used off-label to manage the hyponatraemia of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). Absorption is reduced by dairy products, antacids and iron, so it is taken on an empty stomach.
indications: Rickettsial infections - Rocky Mountain spotted fever, typhus group, Q fever, rickettsialpox, tick fevers
Respiratory tract infections caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Chlamydial infections - lymphogranuloma venereum, psittacosis, trachoma, inclusion conjunctivitis, non-gonococcal urethritis
Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis), chancroid, plague, tularaemia, cholera, brucellosis (with streptomycin), bartonellosis, granuloma inguinale
Infections by susceptible gram-negative organisms (E. coli, Enterobacter, Shigella, Acinetobacter, Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella) when bacteriologically confirmed
Infections by susceptible gram-positive organisms (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus) when penicillin is contraindicated
Off-label: chronic hyponatraemia due to SIADH

dosage.d: Four divided doses of 150 mg each, or two divided doses of 300 mg each (about 600 mg/day)
dosage.n: Continue for at least 24-48 h after symptoms and fever subside

dosage.d: Initial 600 mg orally, then 300 mg every 12 h for 4 days (total 3 g)
dosage.n: Confirm susceptibility; follow current STI guidance

dosage.d: 7 to 13 mg/kg/day depending on severity, divided into 2-4 doses; not exceeding 600 mg/day
dosage.n: Contraindicated in children under 8 years (tooth discoloration)

dosage.d: Typically 600-1200 mg/day in divided doses, titrated to serum sodium
dosage.n: Off-label use; effect via reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; monitor sodium and renal function

admin: Take on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals
Avoid concurrent dairy products, antacids containing aluminium/calcium/magnesium, and iron preparations, which reduce absorption by more than 50%
Swallow with a full glass of water (at least 120 mL) and do not take immediately before lying down to reduce oesophageal irritation/ulceration
Counsel on sun protection because of marked photosensitivity
Do not use beyond the expiry date - degraded tetracyclines have been associated with Fanconi-type renal injury
Reduce the total dose by lowering individual doses or extending intervals in renal or hepatic impairment
moa: Demeclocycline is a bacteriostatic tetracycline that reversibly binds the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, blocking the attachment of aminoacyl-transfer RNA to the messenger RNA-ribosome complex and thereby inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. It has a broad spectrum against many gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, rickettsiae, mycoplasmas, chlamydiae and spirochaetes. Independently of its antibacterial action, demeclocycline antagonises the renal tubular action of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), producing a reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; this water-losing effect is the basis for its off-label use in raising serum sodium in SIADH.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to demeclocycline or any tetracycline
Pregnancy (and latter half of pregnancy in particular)
Children under 8 years of age (tooth discoloration and effects on bone)
relative: Renal impairment (risk of accumulation and azotaemia)
monitor: Liver function on prolonged or high-dose therapy
Serum sodium and renal function when used for SIADH
Full blood count on long-term use

preg: Demeclocycline, like other tetracyclines, can cause fetal harm. Use during the latter half of pregnancy causes permanent discoloration of the deciduous teeth and may impair fetal skeletal development; animal data show embryotoxicity. It is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no safer alternative exists for a serious infection.
lact: Tetracyclines are excreted into breast milk and can theoretically cause tooth staining and effects on bone in the infant, although calcium chelation limits absorption. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during demeclocycline therapy.
renal: Demeclocycline is partly renally cleared and its anti-anabolic action raises blood urea nitrogen. In significant renal impairment, accumulation can lead to azotaemia, hyperphosphataemia, acidosis and possible liver toxicity. Reduce the total dose by lowering individual doses or extending dosing intervals and monitor renal function; note that this drug also induces a reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
hepatic: Tetracyclines, including demeclocycline, are concentrated in the liver and excreted in bile and can cause hepatotoxicity, particularly at high doses or in renal impairment. Use cautiously in hepatic impairment, reduce the dose, and avoid high cumulative doses.

major: Oral retinoids (e.g. isotretinoin) - additive risk of benign intracranial hypertension; avoid concurrent use
Penicillins - tetracyclines may antagonise the bactericidal action of penicillins
moderate: Polyvalent cations (antacids with aluminium/calcium/magnesium, iron, zinc, sucralfate, bismuth) - chelation markedly reduces absorption; separate dosing
Warfarin - tetracyclines may potentiate anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Combined oral contraceptives - possible reduced efficacy (use additional precautions)
Methoxyflurane - risk of fatal nephrotoxicity with tetracyclines
Diuretics - may worsen rise in blood urea nitrogen
minor: May affect requirements for insulin/oral hypoglycaemics in diabetes
interactions.food: Dairy products and food reduce absorption; take on an empty stomach away from milk
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; limit alcohol if hepatic function is impaired
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false elevations of urinary catecholamines; can raise BUN and serum uric acid; long-term use causes microscopic brown-black thyroid discoloration without altering thyroid function tests

common: Gastrointestinal upset - anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
Tooth discoloration if used during tooth development
serious: Hepatotoxicity including rare hepatitis and liver failure
Acute renal failure and rise in BUN (dose-related)
Pseudotumor cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension) in adults; bulging fontanelles in infants
Severe hypersensitivity - anaphylaxis, angio-oedema, lupus-like syndrome, pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia
emergency: Raised intracranial pressure with visual loss

monitoring: Renal function (BUN, creatinine) during prolonged therapy
Liver function tests during prolonged or high-dose therapy
Full blood count on long-term use
Serum sodium and fluid balance when used off-label for SIADH
Visual symptoms suggestive of raised intracranial pressure
counsel: Take on an empty stomach with plenty of water, and do not lie down straight afterwards
Avoid taking it within a few hours of milk, indigestion remedies, or iron and calcium supplements
Use sunscreen and protective clothing - your skin may burn much more easily in sunlight
Tell your doctor if you become pregnant; this medicine must not be used in pregnancy or in young children
Report severe headache with blurred vision, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or persistent diarrhoea
Complete the full prescribed course even if you feel better
pk: Bacteriostatic effect over hours; absorption slower than tetracycline
Peak serum concentration about 4 hours after an oral dose
Long-acting, allowing twice-daily dosing for infection
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from light and moisture; do not use after expiry
pearls: Long-acting tetracycline - can be dosed twice daily (300 mg BID) as well as four times daily
Characteristically induces reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus - basis for off-label use in SIADH hyponatraemia
Contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8 years (permanent tooth discoloration, bone effects)
Marked photosensitivity - counsel on sun protection
Absorption is reduced more than 50% by dairy, antacids and iron - separate dosing and take on empty stomach
Use cautiously and reduce dose in renal impairment - anti-anabolic effect raises BUN and risks azotaemia
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but skip it if it is almost time for the next dose - do not double up. Try to keep the doses evenly spaced and complete the whole course.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe gastrointestinal upset and worsening of hepatic and renal toxicity. There is no specific antidote; discontinue the drug and treat symptomatically with supportive care. Tetracyclines are not removed in significant amounts by haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
